## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Dhammika Sutta* (Snp 2.14) is the fourteenth discourse of the Cūḷavagga in the *Suttanipāta* [Shigaraki and Matsumoto 2013; Saddhatissa 2013]. Set at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove at Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery, the text begins when the lay follower Dhammika visits the Buddha together with five hundred companions to inquire into the proper mode of life [Saddhatissa 2013]. In response, the Buddha delivers a comprehensive exposition setting forth synopses of conduct for both the monastic community and householders [Saddhatissa 2013], outlining the proper ethical code for lay followers of the Dhamma [SuttaCentral]. Modern scholars highlight the sutta—alongside texts such as the *Mahāmaṅgala Sutta* and *Siṅgālovāda Sutta*—as an essential early source for positive, constructive formulations of Buddhist morality [Kalupahana 1976]. In an analysis of verse Sn 387, Daniel M. Stuart observes that the Buddha's injunction to practice the "pure/purifying teaching" (*dhammaṃ dhutaṃ*) presents *dhuta* as something clean and free from defilements to be cultivated, reflecting an early stage of ascetic ideology prior to the formalized lists of *dhutaṅga* practices [Stuart 2012].
SuttaCentral lists no direct curated cross-canonical parallels for the discourse [SuttaCentral]. However, DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse, recording 94 matches across 22 texts [DharmaNexus]. Substantial verse sequences defining the precepts and observance practices (§26.1–27.4) closely match discourses in the *Aṭṭhakanipāta* (AN 8.42) and *Tikanipāta* (AN 3.70), and are cited in commentaries such as the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, and *Parivāra-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Its introductory prose framework (§1.1–1.3) also shares formulaic material with Snp 3.10 (*Kokālika Sutta*), SN 2.21, and MN 146 (*Nandakovāda Sutta*) [DharmaNexus]. In addition, DharmaNexus aligns individual doctrinal passages with Tibetan translations of Mahāyāna texts (including the *Brahmaparipṛcchā*, D0158, and the *Ugraparipṛcchā*, D0063) and the Chinese *Brahmajāla* translation (T 21) [DharmaNexus].
